problem: Navigation and manipulation are handled by separate models or cascaded pipelines, while VLA models that unify them are heavy, data-hungry and fail zero-shot in novel scenes. Prior diffusion policies (NoMaD, Diffusion Policy) are task-specific to either navigation or manipulation.
motivation: Mobile manipulators and humanoids need one lightweight model that plans both meter-scale motion and centimeter-scale pre-grasp approach, at high frequency and onboard. The authors observe that image-space trajectory diffusion with explicit geometric cues (traversability, attention) can be shared across tasks and self-supervised from a few minutes of video.
key_idea: A single RGB-only image-space diffusion policy is switched between navigation and pre-grasping by multi-scale FiLM conditioning on task mode, depth scale and AnyTraverse-derived spatial attention, with depth predicted only along trajectory waypoints.
insight: Explicit geometric structure (traversability and attention maps from AnyTraverse as auto-supervision and conditioning) lets a tiny model trained on ~20 min of video generalize to novel scenes where a GR00T VLA fails. Context conditioning alone gives task-appropriate precision (4.71 cm pre-grasp goal error vs 29.68 cm navigation). No ablations are reported, so the contribution of each component (FiLM, trajectory-aligned depth, scale weighting) is not isolated.
method: Diffusion policy: UNet denoises an image-space trajectory (start/goal/path channels) conditioned on RGB and context c, trained with the standard epsilon-prediction loss, DDPM sampling at inference.

Multi-scale FiLM context: c = [task-mode embedding || depth-scale embedding (meter/cm) || attention-map encoding]; FiLM applied at four encoder scales (64,32,16,8) with spatially varying gamma/beta from attention masks.
Learned task-scale weights: a K×L matrix W initialized so pre-grasp favors fine scales (1.0/0.5) and navigation favors coarse scales, then optimized end-to-end.

Goal learning via attention: a ViT encoder predicts traversability and attention maps; GT goals come from AnyTraverse (object-directed if an object is detected, else traversability-directed forward region). Zero-shot goals for novel objects use feature matching with a reference image.

Trajectory-aligned depth: depth is predicted only at the trajectory waypoints (L1 loss); GT from ML-Depth-Pro for navigation and stereo depth / object poses for pre-grasping; enables collision checking without a depth sensor.
Auxiliary losses: BCE on traversability and L2 on attention; total loss = diff + 0.1 depth + 0.5 trav + 0.3 attn.

Self-supervised data and adaptation: trajectories are generated automatically from AnyTraverse maps with no teleoperation; a new task needs 5 min of video and 10 epochs of fine-tuning (~15-20 min on an RTX 4090).

setting.backbone: Custom UNet diffusion policy with FiLM + ViT encoder (trained from scratch/with frozen visual encoder); AnyTraverse and ML-Depth-Pro used for supervision only
setting.model_size: not stated; 2.0 GB inference memory, 6 GB during training
setting.training_data: ~20 min of self-supervised RGB video (30 Hz) from a humanoid across corridors, tables and tabletop scenes; auto-labelled by AnyTraverse and depth models; 5 min per new task for fine-tuning
setting.observation: monocular RGB (64x64 input) only at inference
setting.action_space: image-space trajectory waypoints (start, goal, path) with predicted depth, converted to robot motion
setting.privileged: none at test time (known object GT poses used only for training-time cm-scale depth supervision)

numbers_note: No standard benchmark; only small real-world trials on Unitree G1 (exploration SR 100 vs NoMaD 93, clearance 2.98 m vs 2.24 m; autonomous goal SR 100, 0.29 m; provided goal SR 52, 0.35 m vs NoMaD 60, 0.5 m; pre-grasp 70.6% goal success, 4.71 cm error). None map to a canonical benchmark, so none are listed.
results: In real-world tests on a Unitree G1, the model reaches 100% collision-free exploration (clearance 2.98 m vs NoMaD's 93% and 2.24 m) and 100% autonomous goal-directed navigation at 0.29 m. With provided goal images it gets 52% at 0.35 m vs NoMaD's 60% at 0.5 m. Pre-grasping reaches 70.6% goal success with 4.71 cm mean error, while GR00T n1.5 got 40% in real-world tests after training on 1,100 demonstrations and GR00T n1.6 failed to generalize zero-shot.
limitations: Depends on AnyTraverse for supervision and has no force feedback
Small-scale real-world evaluation (few trials, n=8 for goal accuracy), no ablations and no standard benchmarks; the goal-image navigation result is below NoMaD
Trained on two scenes with 64x64 inputs; the GR00T comparison is partly anecdotal and uses different tasks
